title: Age at onset of alcohol use and its association with DSM-IV alcohol abuse and dependence: Results from the National Longitudinal Alcohol Epidemiologic Survey

claims.statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether drinking at a young age causes alcohol problems in adulthood, or whether the same family, genetic and personal factors lead to both. In a 1992 US national household survey (NLAES; 42,862 adults interviewed once; about 92% of selected households and 97.4% of selected people took part), the 27,616 adults who had ever drunk were asked how old they were when they first started drinking, not counting tastes or sips: lifetime DSM-IV alcohol dependence was reported by 40.6% to 47.3% of those who recalled starting at 14 or younger, 16.6% of those who started at 18 and 7.9% of those who started at 25 or older (with a rise to 14.7% and 13.6% at 23 and 24), and lifetime abuse without dependence by up to 13.8% (a first drink at 14) against 2.5% (25 or older). After adjustment for sex, race, age group, family history of alcoholism, duration of drinking and current or former drinking, the odds of lifetime dependence were 14% lower, and of abuse 8% lower, for each later year of the first drink, with no confidence intervals or unadjusted estimates given. The age of the first drink was recalled in the same interview as the diagnoses, often decades later; conduct problems, other psychiatric disorders, family environment and other drug use were not measured; two of the adjustments (current or former drinking, and the duration of drinking up to the last drink) may themselves follow from the disorder; and people who had died, were in institutions or were homeless were not sampled. The authors call the age of the first drink a powerful predictor and ages 16 and younger a particularly vulnerable period, but their closing paragraph says that the delay itself or, more likely, other associated factors may explain the link and that a prospective study is needed to tell (Grant & Dawson, 1997). In general-population cohorts that recorded the age of the first drink during adolescence, an earlier first drink went with more adult drinking or alcohol problems in some analyses and not in others, and the association often shrank when other risk factors were taken into account. A systematic review found only four such cohorts up to January 2013 (two in the USA and two in Norway; 447 to 1,311 people each; five reports; no meta-analysis; confidence in the review rated critically low on its study card): in an Oslo school cohort, a later first drink went with less drinking and fewer problems at 18 to 21, with control only for parents' and peers' influence; in a US community cohort, a first drink before 11 went with problem drinking by 31 (odds ratios 2.39 and 5.75, depending on where the first drink happened, against a first drink at 11 or later at a family gathering) but not after adjustment for further risk factors, while feeling drunk at the first drink remained a predictor; in the Young in Norway cohort, drinking by 13 to 14, compared with a later first drink, went with frequent intoxication (odds ratio 1.5, 95% CI 1.2 to 1.9) and with an AUDIT score of 8 or more, a screen for risky drinking (1.6, 1.3 to 2.1), at 26 to 27, adjusted for gender, both falling to 1.2 (0.9 to 1.6) when conduct problems in adolescence were also taken into account; in a Seattle cohort of people who started drinking before 21, the age of the first drink was not associated with adult alcohol misuse or with alcohol dependence at any follow-up, but, compared with a first drink at 11 to 14, a first drink before 11 went with a past-year dependence diagnosis at more of the interviews held every 3 years from 21 to 33 (odds ratio 1.68) and, in a later report, with more chronic dependence, essentially unchanged across four adjusted models. The review's abstract says that rigorous adjustment markedly weakens or removes such associations, which its own Seattle summary contradicts; the authors conclude that it is not yet known whether starting earlier leads to adult problems, and found that feeling drunk at the first drink and the start of regular drinking went with adult problems more strongly than the age of the first drink (Maimaris & McCambridge, 2014). In a Minnesota cohort of twins born 1977 to 1984 (1,512 twins at about age 11; drinking reported at the assessment planned for age 14, held at a mean age of 14.8; outcomes at about 25), twins who had drunk without their parents' permission by that assessment already differed beforehand from twins who had not, notably in delinquent behaviour and in their parents' drinking and smoking; after weighting for 29 characteristics of the twins and their families measured at about 11, early drinking was associated with a higher adult alcohol-use score (standardized coefficient 0.57, SE 0.06), and within twin pairs who differed in early drinking the association was a little over a third as large but remained (0.21, SE 0.09, in all pairs; 0.22, SE 0.10, in identical pairs, who share all their genes and their family; the estimates for identical and fraternal pairs did not differ significantly), whereas within identical pairs early drinking was not clearly associated with symptoms of alcohol abuse or dependence (0.17, SE 0.14) (Irons et al., 2015). Twin comparisons remove what co-twins share, not differences between them such as their own early use of tobacco or other drugs. The same survey's analysis for other drugs is in the answer on starting to use drugs young (Grant & Dawson, 1998). Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
claims.magnitude: Not estimable as a causal effect. Grant & Dawson (1997), NLAES 1992, 27,616 people who had ever drunk, weighted prevalence of lifetime DSM-IV alcohol dependence by recalled age at first drink (SE): 12 or younger 40.6% (2.1), 13 47.3% (2.7), 14 40.8% (1.9), 15 38.7%, 16 30.6%, 17 24.5%, 18 16.6%, 19 16.5%, 20 11.4%, 21 10.0%, 22 9.5%, 23 14.7%, 24 13.6%, 25 or older 7.9% (0.6); lifetime abuse without dependence 8.3% to 13.8% for a first drink at 16 or younger and 2.5% at 25 or older; adjusted odds 14% lower for dependence and 8% lower for abuse per later year of the first drink (odds ratios about 0.86 and 0.92, editors' conversion on the study card), no intervals, p values or unadjusted estimates. Maimaris & McCambridge (2014), four cohorts, no pooling: Oslo (n = 522) structural coefficients −3.465 for debut age on consumption and −13.828 on a problem index (p < 0.0001), with parental and peer control only; Rutgers (n = 447, people with data at every wave) first drink before 11, OR 2.39 (95% CI 1.10–5.20) at a family gathering and 5.75 (1.53–21.54) elsewhere, both against a first drink at 11 or older at a family gathering, for lifetime problem drinking by 31, not significant in the fully adjusted model (coefficient −0.0631), feeling drunk at the first drink 0.3848 (p < 0.0001); Seattle (n = 808 who started drinking before 21), against a first drink at 11–14, for a first drink before 11, at 15–17 and at 18–20: misuse at any follow-up ORs 0.96, 1.40 and 0.64, dependence at any follow-up 1.49, 1.16 and 0.35 (all p > 0.05); first drink before 11 and the number of interviews (every 3 years from 21 to 33) with a past-year dependence diagnosis OR 1.68 (p < 0.05; no intervals), later report (n = 706) chronicity β 0.44 unadjusted and 0.45 to 0.53 in four adjusted models; Young in Norway (n = 1,311), drinking by 13–14 against later, adjusted for gender: frequent intoxication OR 1.5 (1.2–1.9) and AUDIT 8 or more 1.6 (1.3–2.1); both 1.2 (0.9–1.6) with conduct problems added. Irons et al. (2015), drinking without parental permission by the age-14 assessment (mean age 14.8), standardized β (SE): adult alcohol-use index, weighted 0.57 (0.06), within all discordant pairs 0.21 (0.09), identical pairs 0.22 (0.10), fraternal pairs 0.20 (0.14) (within-pair estimates 0.37 and 0.39 of the weighted one, editors' calculation; zygosity did not significantly moderate any within-pair effect); alcohol abuse or dependence symptoms, weighted 0.36, all pairs 0.24 (0.11), identical 0.17 (0.14), fraternal 0.34 (0.16); intoxication by the age-14 assessment and alcohol abuse or dependence symptoms within all pairs 0.29 (0.15). The twin study's printed p-values are not used (card reporting issue).
